text: Apixaban (brand name Eliquis) interruption before an elective procedure: for a low bleeding risk procedure omit apixaban for 1 day before surgery (last dose at least 24 hours before); for a high bleeding risk procedure omit for 2 days (last dose at least 48 hours before). No heparin bridging is needed.

Rivaroxaban (brand name Xarelto) interruption before an elective procedure: low bleeding risk procedure, stop 1 day before (at least 24 hours from last dose); high bleeding risk procedure, stop 2 days before (at least 48 hours from last dose). Bridging anticoagulation is not recommended.
Edoxaban (brand name Savaysa) before surgery: interrupt 1 day before a low bleeding risk procedure and 2 days before a high bleeding risk procedure, i.e. at least 24 or 48 hours after the last dose.

Dabigatran (brand name Pradaxa) in patients with creatinine clearance of 50 mL/min or more: stop 1 day before a low bleeding risk procedure (24 hours) and 2 days before a high bleeding risk procedure (48 hours).

Dabigatran (brand name Pradaxa) with reduced renal function, creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min: drug clearance is prolonged, so stop 2 days before a low bleeding risk procedure (48 hours) and 4 days before a high bleeding risk procedure (96 hours).
Warfarin (brand name Coumadin) (vitamin K antagonist) should be stopped 5 days before an elective procedure, at least 120 hours before surgery, to allow the INR to normalise.
Clopidogrel (brand name Plavix) (P2Y12 inhibitor) should be stopped 5 days before a major elective procedure (at least 120 hours) to limit platelet inhibition at the time of surgery.

Resuming a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) after the procedure: restart no earlier than 1 day (24 hours) after a low bleeding risk procedure and no earlier than 2 days (48 hours) after a high bleeding risk procedure, once haemostasis is secured.
For patients interrupting warfarin, check the INR within 48 hours before surgery; proceed when the INR is 1.5 or lower. An INR above 1.5 before surgery is a discrepancy that needs review.
Before an invasive procedure a platelet count from the previous 7 days should be available; a count below 50 x10^9/L is a contraindication to proceeding without review.
Heparin bridging during warfarin interruption is not routinely recommended for patients with atrial fibrillation; consider it only for mechanical heart valves or recent venous thromboembolism.
Low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention can usually be continued around minor procedures; for major surgery interruption 7 days before may be considered when bleeding risk is high.
Neuraxial anaesthesia requires longer anticoagulant-free intervals and specific timing of catheter removal; follow anaesthesia society guidance.

Procedures are classified by bleeding risk: low (e.g. colonoscopy with biopsy or polypectomy, endoscopy, cataract surgery, dental extraction, skin biopsy) and high (e.g. major abdominal resection such as colectomy, cardiac, intracranial, spinal surgery such as laminectomy, and major orthopaedic surgery such as hip or knee arthroplasty). When the class is unknown, treat the procedure as high bleeding risk.
Routine pre-operative coagulation testing is not required for patients on direct oral anticoagulants when interruption intervals are followed.
Post-operative venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with low-dose heparin may start 6 to 12 hours after surgery when therapeutic anticoagulation is not yet resumed.
Creatinine clearance is estimated from age, weight, sex and serum creatinine using the Cockcroft-Gault equation and guides renally cleared drug timing.
If the INR remains elevated the day before surgery, low-dose oral vitamin K may be given to bring it into range.
